opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to the fact that grantmaking in a field like AI safety is fundamentally a bet on a picture of the world. When you fund something, you're implicitly saying, "I think this matters, I think this is how progress happens, and I think this person or team is well positioned to make it." If you're just deferring to whoever sounds most confident in the room, you end up with a portfolio that's kind of incoherent: a patchwork of other people's priorities without any underlying model tying it together.

And especially early on, when I was working on things like the biological anchors report, a big motivation was that we were being asked to make really large decisions about how much to invest in AI risk, and on what timeline, and there just wasn't a solid, legible case that we could point to. There were people with strong intuitions, but those intuitions were often hard to interrogate. So doing the work myself was partly about figuring out what I actually believed, but it was also about creating something other people could argue with. Once you've written down your assumptions and put numbers on them, someone can say, "I think you're wrong about this specific parameter," and that's a much more productive conversation than two people just trading vibes.

There's also a practical grantmaking reason. When you have your own model, you can evaluate proposals much more sharply. You can ask, "What would have to be true for this to be really valuable?" and then check whether you believe those things. Without that, you tend to over-index on credentials or on how polished the pitch is, and you miss the weird, high-upside projects that don't look impressive on paper but are actually targeting something important.

And honestly, I think it keeps you honest with yourself. It's very easy in this space to feel like you're doing good work because you're moving money around and talking to smart people. But if you haven't done the thinking, you don't really know whether you're helping. Forming your own views, even imperfect ones, at least gives you something to be wrong about, and that means you can notice when you're wrong and update.

r001.rationale: The response says her own model helps her evaluate proposals and identify promising projects, but does not say that it enables her to co-create grant opportunities with researchers or align those opportunities with her goals.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's partly temperament and partly a bet about what actually makes grantmaking work.

On the temperament side, I just find it really hard to move money on the basis of a view I don't understand. If someone tells me "this research direction is important" and I can't reconstruct why, I don't have any way to tell whether the next proposal in that area is good or bad, or whether the field has moved on and that reasoning no longer applies. I'd be pattern-matching on vibes and reputation, and I think that goes wrong in subtle ways that you don't notice until much later.

But the bigger reason is that in AI safety specifically, there isn't really a mature field with settled consensus you can defer to. The questions we care about, like how fast capabilities are going to improve, or what alignment problems are going to be the binding constraint, or which research agendas actually have a shot at helping, those are genuinely contested. The experts disagree with each other, and a lot of the people with the strongest opinions have obvious incentives. So if you're not forming your own views, you're not actually deferring to "the experts," you're deferring to whichever expert you happened to talk to most recently, or whoever is most confident and charismatic. That's a pretty bad aggregation mechanism.

Doing the work myself, writing things up, trying to build explicit models of timelines or of what a particular research bet is supposed to accomplish, forces me to notice where the arguments are actually load-bearing and where they're hand-wavy. And it means when I'm wrong, I can tell what I was wrong about. I've changed my mind on a lot of things over the years, and I think that's only possible because I had something concrete enough to be falsified.

The other thing I'd say is that it's not just about my own decisions. When you write up your reasoning publicly, other people can push on it. A lot of the most useful updates I've gotten came from people reading something I wrote and saying "this step doesn't follow" or "you're missing this consideration." You can't get that feedback on a view that lives entirely in your head as a gut feeling. So forming your own views and making them legible is kind of the same thing as participating in the field rather than just funding it from the outside.

I don't want to overstate it, though. There are lots of areas where I do mostly defer, because I don't have the bandwidth to go deep and there's someone I trust who has. The skill is figuring out which questions are the ones where your own judgment is actually the bottleneck, and spending the effort there.

r001.rationale: The response explains that forming and sharing her own views improves grant decisions and invites feedback, but it does not say this enables her to co-create grant opportunities with researchers that better align with her goals.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the value of being a grantmaker comes from being able to support something that isn’t already obviously good to everybody. If you’re mostly relying on whether other people are excited about a project, you can end up funding things that would have gotten funded anyway, and missing things that are promising but unconventional.

Having your own view gives you a basis for saying, “I can see why people are skeptical of this, but here’s why I think it’s worth trying.” It also lets you engage more substantively with the person doing the work: what are they trying to accomplish, what would have to be true for it to work, and what might we learn even if it doesn’t?

That doesn’t mean ignoring other people’s judgment. I want to learn a lot from other people. But I want to understand the reasoning well enough that I can tell where I agree, where I’m uncertain, and what would change my mind.

r001.rationale: The response says having her own view supports more substantive discussion with researchers, but it does not say they co-create grant opportunities or that those opportunities better align with her goals.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that making grants is fundamentally about making bets under uncertainty. You’re trying to figure out which problems matter, which approaches could make progress, and which people could do something unusually valuable. If you’re relying on other people’s conclusions without understanding why they believe them, it’s hard to know when those conclusions apply to the particular decision in front of you.

And a lot of the value of philanthropy can come from funding things that aren’t already a consensus choice. That doesn’t mean being contrarian for its own sake. It means having enough of your own understanding that you can recognize a promising idea even when it doesn’t have much institutional support—and also explain what would change your mind.

I still want to learn a lot from other people. Forming my own views is more about being able to engage with their reasoning, ask useful questions, and take responsibility for the decision.

r001.rationale: The candidate says forming her own views helps assess uncertain bets, recognize promising ideas, engage with others’ reasoning, and take responsibility. It does not say this enables her to co-create grant opportunities with researchers or align them with her goals.
